body:
It was quite a challenge to understand the underlying issue of your project. Thanks for this very interesting MRP!

The way you implemented input-event propagation is not supported by Godot, because the different systems of mouse to subviewport propagation and mouse-over handling interfere with each other.
Basically, the `SubViewportContainer` connects the mouse-over state of its `SubViewport` child to the mouse-over state of the parent root viewport. This interferes with your intended goal.


I can provide you with two alternatives of how to achieve your goal:

1. Replace the `SubViewportContainer` by a `TextureRect` and set its texture to the `SubViewport` texture.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/11618eb3-c192-4ec3-8736-18ca62426e07)

This will work, because in that case the mouse-over-state of the `SubViewport` is not set automatically by a parent `SubViewportContainer`. Also you don't need the automatic input event propagation of the `SubViewportContainer`.


2. Place the test button in a separate `SubViewport` inside the `SubViewportContainer` and set `SubViewportContainer.mouse_filter` to not IGNORE and remove the `_vp.push_input(event)` in your `Node3D` node

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/322e2423-4a8f-4343-8f8e-1dfaef3787bd)

This will work, because in that case the `SubViewportContainer` treats both `SubViewports` equally and takes care of propagating events to both `SubViewport` children.

So I'm not seeing any bug here in Godot, that could be fixed. The MRP causes Godot-systems to interact in non-intended ways.

Thank you for your response @Sauermann I tried solution number 1 and it worked the way I intended with my project but I still had to call `push_input(event)` on unhandled_input otherwise the controls on the viewport would not receive any event signals. The goal here is to have two 'planes' of controls, one on top of each other, both receiving mouse input events.

This leaves me feeling slightly frustrated, as to why that works but having what I would imagine would be the natural solution, to place it within a SubViewportContainer, does not and this being marked as `wontfix`. Perhaps some documentation on what makes SubViewportContainer special might be warranted.

Regardless, thank you for the quick response and I'm glad to have a working solution.

Edit: Unfortunately it seems like I spoke too soon, when I maximize my project my input breaks. I will try to update my MRP to reflect the issue.

Hello @Sauermann  I have updated this MRP to showcase the issue and why neither TextureRect nor a separate Viewport are unfortunately non-working solutions. I can file another issue if needed.

Edit: The reason a separate viewport won't work is I have some 3d pickable objects in the base node3d scene.

After playing around with the TextureRect solution some more, I noticed that it appears that the viewport isn't updating when the window is resized as I can still move my mouse to the top-left corner and the button goes to the 'hover' state. Is there a way I can manually scale the viewport to match the resolution of the TextureRect?

[test-game-project.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18383036/test-game-project.zip)

Edit: Success (I think?) if I manually update the viewport size on window resize it works the way I intended:

`get_tree().get_root().size_changed.connect(func(): _vp.size = get_viewport().size)`

I'm not 100% sure if this is the correct solution with what I am trying to accomplish. I am making a 3d top-down simulation game that is heavy on the UI, but also allows for 3d object picking along with some control UI. Instead of using the project settings viewport stretch modes (which can either result in blackbars or some stretching of the 3d background scene), I'm creating a viewport that scales proportionally with the game window. I think perhaps if I move all controls to the UI scene that might work best, but I'll continue to test things. If anyone else is having the same issue, the above line of code in the main scene's _ready method ultimately worked for me.

Your explanation helped me to understand your use-case better and there is an even simpler option: use a canvas layer instead of a separate viewport:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e9de31c5-3e56-4ddf-9d73-b0814558d0e3)

That way you can separate the different gui elements and also don't need to deal with SubViewport sizes and input propagation. They are the recommended way to take care of stationary GUI elements, that are independent of 3D-camera views.

This use-case is also mentioned in the docs here: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/2d/canvas_layers.html#canvaslayers

Thanks @Sauermann for your responses and I apologize if it is frustrating answering these questions.

Unfortunately, I tried using a CanvasLayer but it's missing a critical feature that the Viewport solves which is proportional scaling based on the window size. My goal is to create one UI size and run the application on different display devices/resolutions without needing to calculate different font sizes and other things.

Canvas Layer:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f1b4c74b-05cb-49b7-a2cc-5dab746fdaf4)

Viewport Scaling:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8da4527a-f1e8-4e21-b961-a985483fa41a)

While this does have some obvious drawbacks, in that the scaled UI will get blurry after awhile and there is some UI stretching if I play with the window size a bit, it does work well with my specific use case of running this on my desktop, laptop, and steam deck with relatively decent scaled UI to the device without any blackbars.

CanvasLayer with better attention to how the UI scales is probably the more correct solution in the long run so I will continue to test things. Thank you for you help!

Edit: I absolutely concede that I probably am not fully understanding the fundamental issues at work here and my solution is a bad hack.
